title: Grade 3 Two Step Word Problems: How to Solve Them + Free Quiz
meta_title: Grade 3 Two Step Word Problems (How to Solve)
meta_desc: Teach your child grade 3 two step word problems the easy way: break into step 1 and step 2, spot the hidden question, and check. Free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: The jump from one-step to two-step word problems is where most Grade 3 children stumble. Here is the exact routine I use to break a problem into step 1 and step 2, plus a quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Rohan buys 3 pens at ₹12 each and pays with a ₹50 note. How much change does he get back? A child who has just mastered one-step sums will often blurt out ₹38 — they subtracted 12 from 50 and forgot there were three pens. That single miss is the whole story of grade 3 two step word problems: the maths is easy, but the answer hides behind a second question the child never noticed. Getting past this is less about arithmetic and more about slowing down and reading like a detective.

By now your child can handle single-operation problems — add these, subtract those, multiply, share equally. This post assumes that. What changes in Grade 3 is that one answer becomes the raw material for the next. You multiply to find the cost, then subtract to find the change. Two operations, one problem, and an in-between number nobody asks for out loud.

What makes a two-step problem different

In a one-step problem the question matches the numbers directly. In a two-step problem there is a gap: the numbers give you something, but not the thing being asked. You have to build a stepping-stone answer first, then use it. I tell children the first answer is a ‘secret number’ — the problem needs it, but the question does not mention it.

Take Rohan again. The question asks for change. To find change you need the total cost. The total cost is not given — you have to make it (3 × 12 = 36). That 36 is the secret number. Only then can you do 50 − 36 = 14. The change is ₹14, not ₹38.

The two-step routine that works

Here is the routine I drill until it becomes automatic. It is deliberately boring — boring is what stops silly mistakes.

  • Read it twice. First read for the story, second read for the actual question at the end. Underline the question.
  • Find the secret number. Ask: ‘What do I need before I can answer this?’ That is step 1.
  • Write step 1 down. Do the first operation and write the answer on its own line. Do not keep it in your head.
  • Do step 2. Use the written step-1 answer to finish the problem.
  • Check the question. Reread the underlined question. Did you answer that, or did you stop halfway?

The line ‘write step 1 down’ sounds trivial. It is the single biggest fix I know. Children who hold the secret number in their head lose it, then answer with whatever number is freshest — usually the last one they read.

Worked examples across operations

Two-step problems mix operations, so practice should too. Here are three, each needing a different pair. Notice how step 1 always feeds step 2.

ProblemStep 1 (secret number)Step 2 (the answer)
Meera has 4 boxes of 8 laddoos. She gives 6 away. How many left?4 × 8 = 32 laddoos32 − 6 = 26 laddoos
A shop sold 45 tickets on Friday and 38 on Saturday, in rows of 5. How many rows?45 + 38 = 83 tickets83 ÷ 5 → 16 rows, 3 left over
Arjun saves ₹15 a week for 6 weeks, then spends ₹40. How much is left?15 × 6 = ₹9090 − 40 = ₹50

See the pattern? The first column never hands you the answer. It hands you a tool. That reframing — step 1 makes a tool, step 2 uses it — is the whole skill.

Spotting the hidden second question

Some problems bury the second step in innocent-looking words. ‘How many more…’, ‘how much change’, ‘how many are left’, ‘share equally after…’ — these phrases almost always signal a second operation coming after a first. Train your child to circle these words. They are the trip-wire that a one-step answer is not enough.

A caveat worth saying out loud

Do not push speed here. A Grade 3 child who writes both steps neatly and takes 90 seconds is in far better shape than one who fires off an answer in ten and gets it wrong half the time. In my experience teaching eight-year-olds, the neat-and-slow group overtakes the fast-and-loose group within a few months, because their method scales to harder problems. Speed is a by-product of a solid method, never a substitute for one.

One more honest trade-off: estimation. It is tempting to teach ‘check by estimating’ straight away, but for most Grade 3 children the reliable check is simpler — reread the question and ask ‘does my number answer this exact thing?’ Estimation as a check can wait until the two-step method itself is secure.

Common mistakes and quick fixes

  • Answering the secret number. The child stops at step 1 (says ₹36 instead of the change). Fix: always reread the underlined question.
  • Using the wrong operation for step 2. Fix: ask ‘am I combining, taking away, grouping, or sharing?’ before writing.
  • Mixing up which number is which. Fix: label the step-1 answer with its unit — ‘32 laddoos’, not just ‘32’.

quiz.about: Grade 3 two-step word problems (two operations each)

questions.q: Rohan buys 3 pens at ₹12 each and pays with ₹50. How much change does he get?
questions.explanation: Step 1: 3 × 12 = ₹36 total. Step 2: 50 − 36 = ₹14 change. The ₹36 is the secret number, not the answer.

questions.q: Meera has 4 boxes with 8 laddoos each. She gives 6 away. How many are left?
A shop sold 45 tickets on Friday and 38 on Saturday. Seats come in rows of 5. How many full rows are sold?
questions.explanation: Step 1: 45 + 38 = 83 tickets. Step 2: 83 ÷ 5 = 16 full rows (with 3 left over).

questions.q: Arjun saves ₹15 each week for 6 weeks, then spends ₹40. How much money is left?
A baker made 60 biscuits and packed 8 in each box. He then sold 5 boxes. How many boxes are unsold?
questions.explanation: Step 1: 60 ÷ 8 gives about 7 full boxes (7 × 8 = 56). Step 2: 7 − 5 = 2 boxes unsold.

questions.q: Priya had 24 stickers. She bought 3 packs of 6 more. How many stickers now?
A class of 32 children is split into 4 equal teams. Then 3 children join each team. How many are in each team now?
questions.explanation: Step 1: 32 ÷ 4 = 8 per team. Step 2: 8 + 3 = 11 per team.

questions.q: A book has 96 pages. Sana read 28 pages, then read 15 more. How many pages are left?
questions.explanation: Step 1: 28 + 15 = 43 pages read. Step 2: 96 − 43 = 53 pages left.

faq.q: What is a two-step word problem in Grade 3?
faq.a: It is a problem that needs two operations to solve, where the first answer feeds the second. For example, multiply to find a total cost, then subtract to find the change. Grade 3 usually mixes add, subtract, multiply and divide across these.

faq.q: Why does my child stop after the first step?
faq.a: Because the first answer feels like an answer — it is a real number the problem produced. The fix is simple: underline the actual question first, then reread it after solving to check you answered that and not the in-between number.

faq.q: Should my child write the first step down or do it mentally?
faq.a: Always write it down, labelled with its unit (like ‘32 laddoos’). Holding the in-between number in your head is the most common cause of wrong answers, because children lose it and finish with whatever number they read last.

faq.q: How do I know if a problem needs two steps?
faq.a: Look for the numbers giving you something the question does not directly ask for. Words like ‘how much change’, ‘how many left’, ‘how many more’ and ‘share equally after…’ usually signal a hidden second step.
